name: Payne's Grey
lede: Payne's Grey is a blue-grey mixed by watercolorists in place of plain black, named for the English painter William Payne around 1800.

sections.title: A painter's substitute for black
sections.body:
William Payne was a British watercolorist, born in Devon around 1760, who worked first as an engineer before teaching watercolor in London [3]. He is credited with mixing a softer, bluish grey to replace the flat, deadening black many of his students reached for in shadows [3]. His original recipe combined Prussian blue, yellow ochre and crimson lake, a far more complex mix than the name's later, simpler recipes suggest [3].

The nearest named colors on file are [[black-coral]] and [[delphinium]], at The ISCC-NBS 1955 revision places it in block 186, "grayish blue," a near-exact match (ΔE 0.4) to the Ridgway chip [1][2]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates the name in English to 1835, decades after Payne's own death [1].

Twentieth-century recipes for "Payne's grey" paint drifted from Payne's own mixture: one later formula swaps in indigo for Prussian blue, and most modern tubes now mix ultramarine with a carbon black instead [3]. The name has outlived the paint it first described.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A screen match for this grey-blue turns up in 270 of 23,781 paintings in our archive, about 1.1 percent, as photographed [2]. It is almost three times more common in paintings from the 1900s decade than the archive's average rate, and leans toward painters working in watery, atmospheric blues: Paul Signac, Paul Sérusier and Claude Monet all carry it well above the archive's base rate [2]. Its single most covered appearance is Whistler's *Violet and Silver—The Deep Sea* (1893), where it fills more than half the canvas [2]. These are computed color matches on photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not identifications of any pigment Payne, Whistler or Monet actually used [2].

openers: Payne's Grey was invented so students would stop reaching for plain black — and the recipe has changed completely since.
